clue.text: Drink beer with fruit

parts.note: bitter is a type of British draught beer, a well-hopped pale ale
a lemon is a sour yellow citrus fruit

explanation.surface: Someone orders a pint served alongside a piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: BITTER is the well-hopped draught ale found in British pubs. Put the fruit after it and you have a mixer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitter lemon is a fizzy soft drink flavoured with lemon and quinine, often used as a mixer.

clue.text: Coming from Orient, bee is something one particularly dislikes

indicators.note: the letters of the following words come out rearranged, as if produced from them

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An insect arriving from the East turns out to be a pet hate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming from' tells you to rearrange ORIENT and BEE together. 'Orient' looks like the East, but here it is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Bête noire, French for 'black beast', is a borrowed phrase for a person or thing you especially detest.

clue.text: Try right away to bring replacement stool in for author

indicators.note: the rearranged stool is put inside the shortened try, so in signals a container
the letter for right is sent away from the word try, leaving its other letters
the word stool is replaced by a new arrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: Someone is told to bring in a new stool for a visiting writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right away' leaves TY, and 'replacement' turns the stool into OLSTO, which 'in' places between those two letters. 'to bring' is linking text, and 'for' introduces the writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Leo Tolstoy was the Russian novelist who wrote War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

clue.text: Takes a look at Conservatives in command

parts.note: to eye something is to look at it, so eyes means takes a look at
the right is the conservative wing of politics

explanation.surface: Someone sizes up the Tories who are now in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in command' reads as Conservatives being in power. In fact 'in' is a link word and 'command' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyes right is a military order on parade, telling troops to turn their heads to the right.

clue.text: Only cranny concealing synthetic fibre

indicators.note: the two words hold the answer inside them, running across the gap between them

explanation.surface: A single crack in a wall has a man-made thread tucked inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concealing' means the fibre is hidden inside 'onLY CRAnny'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lycra is a trade name for spandex, a stretchy man-made fibre used in sportswear.

clue.text: Scotsman has time, very long time to produce picture

parts.note: mon is a Scottish dialect form of man, so a Scotsman can be called mon
an age is a very long stretch of time

explanation.surface: A patient Scot spends ages producing a painting.
explanation.walkthrough: MON is Scots dialect for 'man', a convention setters use for a Scotsman. 'has' and 'to produce' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A montage is a composite picture made by putting together pieces of other images.

clue.text: Foster sister?

explanation.surface: A question about a girl brought up in a foster family.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a foster sibling. Instead, 'Foster' is a verb and 'sister' is a hospital title.
explanation.definitionFit: To nurse a hope is to foster it, and in British hospitals a sister is a senior nurse in charge of a ward.

clue.text: Overweight, a pound more could be deadly

parts.note: someone overweight is fat
L is the abbreviation for pound, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: For someone already overweight, gaining another pound could be a killer.
explanation.walkthrough: L for pound comes from the Latin libra, as in the £ sign. 'more could be' is linking text.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fatal causes death, so it is deadly.

clue.text: Dishonest crustacean?

parts.note: a cheat or swindler is a fiddler, so a shellfish that cheats gets a nickname built on that word; the real creature has one oversized claw like a violinist's bow arm

explanation.surface: A lobster or crab with a shady character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dishonest' points to someone who fiddles, meaning cheats. The question mark shows that a real crustacean is being described in a playful way.
explanation.definitionFit: The fiddler crab is a small shore crab, and the male waves one huge claw as if bowing a violin.

clue.text: Odd not having the same middle

explanation.surface: Something strange because its centre is off.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is the geometric sense: circles that are not concentric.
explanation.definitionFit: Eccentric means strange or unconventional, and in geometry it describes circles or orbits whose centres do not coincide.

clue.text: Woodworker unhesitatingly brings song from Australian gulf

indicators.note: er is the sound of hesitation, so without hesitating the word loses those two letters

parts.note: a carpenter is a craftsman who works with wood
an aria is a solo song in an opera

explanation.surface: A joiner confidently sings a tune that comes from somewhere in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unhesitatingly' drops ER, the written hesitation noise, from CARPENTER and leaves CARPENT. 'brings' and 'from' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gulf of Carpentaria is the large shallow sea inlet on the north coast of Australia.

clue.text: Donald working with gold is the one making the gift

parts.note: Don is a short form of the name Donald
to be at something is to be busy with it, as in hard at it, so at can stand for working
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A man named Donald who works with gold is the generous giver.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is gold in heraldry. AT for 'working' is a loose use, from phrases such as 'at work' and 'hard at it'.
explanation.definitionFit: A donator is a donor, someone who gives a present or contribution.

clue.text: A mature undisciplined sportsman perhaps

indicators.note: letters that are undisciplined are out of order, so the words a mature get rearranged

explanation.surface: A grown-up who lacks discipline, perhaps an athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'undisciplined' rearranges the letters of A MATURE. 'perhaps' shows that the definition is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: An amateur plays without being paid, and a sports player is one common example.

clue.text: Italian to place a bet outside for ordinary people

indicators.note: the betting word goes outside the abbreviation, wrapping round it

parts.note: to lay is to stake money on a wager
IT is a standard abbreviation for Italian, as in It. on labels

explanation.surface: An Italian sets out to bet on behalf of the common folk.
explanation.walkthrough: In betting, to 'lay' a bet means to stake money on it. The wrapping word 'outside' sits after both pieces, which reads naturally.
explanation.definitionFit: The laity are lay people, members of a church or field who are not clergy or experts.

clue.text: Yellow feature of sea-duck

parts.note: golden is a rich yellow colour
an eye is one of the features of the face

explanation.surface: Describing a bird's yellow marking.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a duck's yellow marking, and that is also how the bird got its name. 'of' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: The goldeneye is a diving duck of northern waters, named for its bright yellow iris.

clue.text: Cheap ring?

parts.note: ring here is a phone call rather than jewellery, and calls to nearby numbers used to cost less than long-distance ones

explanation.surface: A bargain piece of jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ring' suggests a piece of jewellery, but it means a telephone call. In Britain a call within your own area used to be charged at a lower rate.
explanation.definitionFit: A local call is a phone call to a number in the same area, traditionally charged at the cheapest rate.

clue.text: Worm-catching satellite

explanation.surface: A satellite that hunts worms.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb says 'the early bird catches the worm'. Early Bird was the 1965 nickname of Intelsat I, the first commercial communications satellite.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb's worm-catcher is the bird that rises first, and Early Bird was the popular name of the first commercial communications satellite.

clue.text: Discharge one with twitch having this fever

parts.note: rheum is a watery discharge from the eyes or nose
a means one, as in a single thing
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: A runny nose plus a nervous twitch are taken as symptoms of a fever.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition depends on rheumatic fever: someone suffering from it is rheumatic. 'with' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheumatic describes someone affected by rheumatism, and rheumatic fever is the inflammatory illness named after that condition.

clue.text: Criminal endlessly vandalising vehicle

indicators.note: the remaining letters are smashed up and rebuilt in a new order
the word criminal loses its end, its final letter

explanation.surface: A crook keeps damaging a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' takes the final L off CRIMINAL, and 'vandalising' rearranges CRIMINA.
explanation.definitionFit: A minicar is a very small car, a type of motor vehicle.

clue.text: Pair during first half of weekend shortly had fish

indicators.note: the abbreviation for pair occurs during, so inside, the shortened day

parts.note: Saturday is the first half of the weekend, and Sat is its short form

explanation.surface: A couple spending Saturday morning eating fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The British weekend is Saturday and Sunday, so its first half is Saturday, and 'shortly' gives its usual abbreviation. 'had' is a link word, and 'fish' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprat is a small silvery fish of the herring family.

clue.text: National topic

explanation.surface: A subject of national interest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'National' is a noun here: a citizen of a country, such as a British national.
explanation.definitionFit: A citizen of a state is one of its subjects, and a topic of discussion is also a subject.

clue.text: Wrote beneath said building

indicators.note: said tells you the phrase is spoken and the spelling follows the sound

parts.note: wrote under, said in a non-rhotic British accent, sounds like the answer

explanation.surface: Someone wrote something underneath a building's name.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'wrote under' in an accent that drops the final R and you hear the domed building.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotunda is a round building, usually topped with a dome.

clue.text: Can journalist be spiked?

parts.note: a tin is a can, as of beans
ED, short for editor, is the usual crossword journalist

explanation.surface: Asking whether a reporter's story could be killed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface uses 'spiked' in its newspaper sense of a story being dropped. Here it means having prongs. 'be' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Tined means fitted with tines, the sharp prongs of a fork or antler, so it means spiked.

clue.text: One part of bird that's causing dread

parts.note: a means one, a single thing
a wing is a part of a bird

explanation.surface: A bird's limb that fills onlookers with fear.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the verb 'awe', inspiring fearful wonder. 'that's' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Awing is the present participle of awe, which means filling someone with reverent fear.

clue.text: One attempting to influence Beryl surprisingly taking old boy in

indicators.note: the rearranged name takes the other piece into itself, so this signals a container
in completes the phrase taking in, meaning the second piece goes inside the first
the name beryl turns out surprisingly, with its letters in a new order

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil of a school

explanation.surface: A woman named Beryl unexpectedly takes in a former schoolboy, perhaps to win favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surprisingly' makes LBYER, and 'taking ... in' places the former pupil just after its first letter. In Britain an old boy is a former pupil of a school.
explanation.definitionFit: A lobbyer is a lobbyist, someone who tries to persuade politicians to support a cause.

clue.text: Skeleton service for use at dinner or tea?

definitions.text: Skeleton service for use at dinner or tea?

parts.words: Skeleton service for use at dinner or tea?
parts.note: skeleton suggests a minimal staff of servers, but it also points to the material, since this fine porcelain is made with ground animal bone

explanation.surface: Restaurant staff cut to the bone for mealtimes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skeleton service' suggests a skeleton staff. In fact 'service' is a set of crockery made from bone.
explanation.definitionFit: Bone china is translucent porcelain made with bone ash, used for fine dinner and tea sets.

clue.text: Lady accepted some esoteric articles

indicators.note: the lady is accepted inside the words that follow, made up of some of their letters

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A woman agreed to take some obscure pieces of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition 'Lady accepted' cannot replace a name in a sentence. 'accepted some' is the hiding signal: the name sits inside esotERIC Articles.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is a woman's name, so it can stand for any lady.

clue.text: Freed from controls of Parisian following routine for the most part, Edward concluded

indicators.note: the short form of Edward concludes the answer, coming at the end

parts.note: de is the French for of, as a Parisian would say it

indicators.note: most of the word is kept, with the final letter dropped

parts.note: regular means routine, done as a matter of habit
Ted is a familiar short form of the name Edward

explanation.surface: Something released from rules because a Frenchman mostly followed habit, as Edward decided.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for the most part' leaves REGULA, and 'concluded' places Edward's short form last. 'following' only joins the pieces and does not change their order.
explanation.definitionFit: Deregulated means having had official rules or restrictions removed.
